title: Correlation Localization in Waveguide QED with Delayed Interactions
authors: N. Vera, F. M. Quinteros, P. Barberis-Blostein, P. Solano
abstract: We study the atom-atom correlation length in an atomic array coupled to a waveguide under the Bragg condition with delayed non-Markovian interactions caused by a finite photon propagation time. Starting from a single excited atom, the excitation partially spreads among all atoms, reaching a steady state. The remaining excitation localizes near the initially excited atom, and the atom-atom correlation length decreases as a power law with the interaction delay. This localization phenomenon reveals how the delay-induced non-Markovian behavior affects the correlation transport in waveguide QED systems.
summary: This paper analyzes excitation dynamics in an atomic array coupled to a waveguide when interactions are delayed (non-Markovian). The key finding is that this delay causes the initially spread excitation to partially localize near the source atom. This localization effect suppresses long-range quantum correlations, with the correlation length scaling inversely with the square root of the interaction delay.
main_problem: The study investigates how delayed, non-Markovian interactions affect the atom-atom correlation length within an array of atoms coupled to a waveguide under Bragg conditions.
main_result: Increased interaction delay causes the excitation probability to localize near the initially excited atom, leading to a power-law decrease in the correlation length ($\xi \propto 	au^{-1/2}$).
method: The authors solve the system dynamics by deriving and numerically solving complex delay differential equations governing the atomic coefficients.
model_or_system: The model is an array of N atoms coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide (wQED) operating in the single-excitation manifold under Bragg conditions. The interactions are non-Markovian due to finite photon propagation time ($	au$).
key_observables: Atom-atom correlation length ($\xi$), steady-state excitation probability of central vs. neighboring atoms, and spin-spin correlation function $g(j)$.
important_parameters: Interaction delay ($	au$ or $\gamma	au$), system size (N), disorder strength ($\sigma$), and the Bragg condition.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the single-excitation manifold, and derivations rely on approximations like extending frequency integration over negative frequencies in the RWA for the delay equation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic setups under Bragg conditions, decay dynamics of excitation probability vs. atom index for varying delays, and log-log plots showing power-law scaling relationships between $\xi$ and both delay ($\gamma	au$) and disorder ($\sigma$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and Hamiltonian to deriving the governing delay differential equations (avoiding Born-Markov), analyzing the Markovian limit, and finally solving for the steady-state localization properties in the non-Markovian regime, including disorder effects.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it explores how retardation effects fundamentally alter quantum transport and coherence preservation in solid-state or waveguide QED systems, providing quantitative scaling laws for correlation decay.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of an atomic array coupled to a waveguide under the Bragg condition, where all atoms are spaced by a distance vτ, with v representing the group velocity and τ the delayed interaction time. The central atom is initially excited, whereas all other atoms are in the ground state. The waveg- uide mediates photon exchange among the atoms, enabling collective dynamics that lead to localization of steady-state atom-atom correlations for large delays.

FIG. 3. a Dynamics of the excitation probability for all neigh- boring atoms (excluding the central atom) as a function of time for γτ = 0.1 and N = 21 atoms. b Steady-state excita- tion probability of the neighboring atoms versus atom index for different values of γτ, illustrating the spatial localization of the remaining excitation around the initially excited atom.

FIG. 2. a Decay dynamics of the central (initially excited) atom for various delayed interaction times τ and N = 21 atoms. Each curve shows how the excitation probability evolves to a steady state. b Steady-state excitation probabil- ity of the central atom as a function of the number of atoms in the system for different delay times. Curves correspond to distinct delays; the gray curve is the analytic Markovian so- lution and the horizontal dashed line marks its infinite-atom limit.

FIG. 4. Correlation length ξ as a function of the delayed interaction parameter γτ shown in a log-log plot. The gray curve illustrates a linear fit, showing that ξ ∼(γτ)−0.48, which suggests that the correlation length scales with the delay ac- cording to a power law. The inset shows the exponential fit to the spin-spin correlation function for the point indicated by an arrow as an example. By employing a sequence of 21 atoms, the simulation ensures that the solution converges and that boundary effects are eliminated.

FIG. 5. Correlation length ξ as a function of the disorder pa- rameter σ shown in a log-log plot. The curves illustrate linear fits, serving as a visual aid, given by ξσ ∼σ−0.75, σ−0.5, σ−0.3, and σ−0.2 with increasing τ. The gray dashed line indicates the approximatzed localization threshold of disorder.
